preamble: The voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] becoming the labio-velar glide [w] combines voicing with loss of friction. Its classic case is the Japanese ha-gyō tenkō ('ha-row shift'): by the 11th century, Old Japanese medial /ɸ/ (from earlier *p) had merged with /w/ between vowels. This is why 'river' is written かは (kafa) in historical kana orthography but is pronounced kawa. Later, /w/ was lost before every vowel except /a/, so most medial ɸ is now zero (iɸe > ie 'house').

examples.note: Intervocalic ɸ merged with w by the 11th century; the historical spelling かは survived until the 1946 kana reform.
The w stage was later lost before o.

sources: Frellesvig, B. (2010). A History of the Japanese Language. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511778322
